Notes: cpp- Class with Pointer

Class with Pointer
When a class contains a pointer as its data member, we need to ensure that
  1. The memory gets allocated separately for each object when they are created.
  2. Every object deletes its own resource pointed by that pointer data member to avoid destruction of memory pointed by pointer data member of other object
  3. While copying one object to another object, separate memory should be allocated for pointer data member of the object and then only data should get copied. (Pointer values should not be copied as it is. Values pointed by the pointer should be copied)

Role of Constructor and Destructor
  • Constructor of a class having pointer as its data member, should first allocate appropriate memory and store its address in the pointer data member. It should then copy the state into this memory.
  • Destructor of a class having pointer as its data member, should delete the memory pointed by this pointer data member, so that there is no memory leakage.
1Class declaration

​Note that:
  • Class CString has pointer p as its data member. It is a char pointer. 
2Writing Constructor

​
  • In the constructor, the pointer data member p, is first allocated appropriate block of memory using new, then values are copied to this newly allocated block of memory.
3Writing Destructor

​
  • In the Destructor, the memory pointed by the data member pointer is deleted using delete. Then the pointer value is set to NULL.
Shallow Copy
In C++, "deep copy" and "shallow copy" are fundamental concepts when dealing with objects that manage dynamically allocated memory or resources. They determine how the data within an object is duplicated when one object is assigned to another or passed as an argument.
What is Shallow copy
A shallow copy creates a new object and copies the values of the member variables from the source object to the destination object. If any of these member variables are pointers, only the addresses that the pointers hold are copied, not the data they point to.

This is represented on memory as shown in the image below.

​
Characteristics of Shallow Copy:
  • Default Behavior: This is the default behavior of the copy constructor and assignment operator generated by the C++ compiler if you don't define your own.
  • Shared Resources: Both the original and the copied object will point to (and thus share) the same dynamically allocated memory or resources.
  • Problematic with Pointers: This can lead to issues like:
    • Double Free: When one object is destroyed, it frees the shared memory. If the other object is later destroyed, it will attempt to free the same memory again, leading to a crash.
    • Dangling Pointers: If one object modifies the shared data, the other object's view of that data also changes, potentially unexpectedly. If one object frees the memory, the other object's pointer becomes "dangling" (pointing to invalid memory).
Deep copy with Copy constructor
A deep copy creates a new object and copies the values of all member variables. More importantly, if any member variables are pointers to dynamically allocated memory, the deep copy allocates new memory for the destination object and then copies the contents of the pointed-to data from the source object to this newly allocated memory.

This is represented on memory as shown in the image below.

​

Characteristics of Deep Copy:
  • Independent Resources: The original and the copied object each have their own independent copies of dynamically allocated memory or resources.
  • Requires Custom Implementation: You must explicitly define your own copy constructor and assignment operator to perform a deep copy.
  • No Double Free: Since each object owns its own memory, there are no double-free issues when objects are destroyed.
  • ​​​​​​​Isolation: Changes to one object's dynamically allocated data do not affect the other object.
    ​​​​​​​
When to use:
Shallow Copy (Default):
  • Suitable when your class does not manage any dynamically allocated memory or resources (e.g., only contains primitive data types or objects that themselves perform deep copies).
  • When you intend for multiple objects to share the same underlying data. (Though this is less common and often requires careful design to avoid issues).

Deep Copy (Custom Implementation):
  • Essential when your class manages dynamically allocated memory (e.g., new/delete, smart pointers, file handles, network connections). This is the most common scenario where you need to consider copy behavior.
  • When you want each object to have its own independent copy of all data, including pointed-to data.
Overloading operators
While writing a class with pointer, we must ensure that resources pointed by the pointer are allocated separately in all objects. No two objects should share same resources, to avoid dangling pointer issues. To ensure this, following are the steps one should follow while writing a class having pointer data member. 
Steps to be followed for writing a Class with pointers

1Declare the Pointer in the Class

class MyClass {
private:
    int* data;  // pointer data member
};

2Allocate Memory in the Constructor

MyClass(int value) {
    data = new int(value);  // allocate memory
}
3Implement a Destructor to Free Memory

~MyClass() {
    delete data;  // release memory
}
4Implement a Copy Constructor (To create a Deep Copy)

MyClass(const MyClass& other) {
    // Allocate separate memory to the pointer data member and initialize it with the other objects state.
    data = new int(*other.data);  // deep copy
}
5Overload the Assignment Operator (To create Deep Copy)

MyClass& operator=(const MyClass& other) {
    if (this != &other) {
        delete data;                 // clean up old memory
        data = new int(*other.data); // deep copy
    }
    return *this;
}
